title: Chemical Analysis and Identification
description: Use chromatography, Rf values, titration apparatus, flame tests, ion tests and gas tests to identify substances and assess purity for Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620, including Extended locating agents and calculations.

notes.heading: Chromatography and Purity
notes.body:
📌 Paper chromatography separates mixtures of soluble substances using a suitable solvent. Draw the baseline in **pencil**, place small concentrated spots on it, and keep the starting solvent level below the spots.

🔑 Interpreting a chromatogram
• A pure substance gives one spot under the same conditions.
• An impure mixture gives more than one spot.
• An unknown matches a known substance if its spot travels the same distance under identical conditions.
• Colourless substances need a **locating agent** after separation so their positions become visible.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Starting with solvent above the baseline: the sample dissolves directly into the solvent reservoir instead of travelling up the paper. Ink is unsuitable for the baseline because its dyes may separate.

📎 Key Points to Remember
Compare chromatograms only under the same conditions, and use spot count to assess purity.

notes.heading: Rf Values: Quantitative Comparison
notes.body:
📌 Extended chromatography uses the retardation factor:
$$R_f = \dfrac{\text{distance travelled by substance}}{\text{distance travelled by solvent}}$$
Measure both distances from the baseline, the substance distance to the centre of its spot and the solvent distance to the solvent front.

💡 Worked Example
A spot moves 4.0 cm while the solvent front moves 8.0 cm: $R_f = 4.0/8.0 = 0.50$. Rf has no units and cannot exceed 1 in a correctly measured chromatogram.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Dividing solvent distance by substance distance or measuring from the bottom of the paper. Both distances start at the baseline.

📎 Key Points to Remember
Use matching units, calculate substance ÷ solvent, and compare Rf values only for the same chromatography conditions.

illustration.alt: A chromatogram with a pencil baseline, a solvent front 8 centimetres above it and a spot centred 4 centimetres above it, giving an Rf value of 0.50.
illustration.caption: Measure from the baseline: Rf = substance distance ÷ solvent-front distance = 4.0 ÷ 8.0 = 0.50.

notes.heading: Acid–Base Titration Technique
notes.body:
📌 A titration finds the volume of one solution that reacts exactly with a measured volume of another.

🔑 Required apparatus
• Use a **volumetric pipette** to transfer an accurate fixed volume, often 25.0 cm³, to a conical flask.
• Add a few drops of a suitable indicator.
• Fill a **burette**, read the starting volume at eye level, and add solution while swirling.
• Near the end-point, add drop by drop until the indicator changes permanently.
• Repeat for concordant titres.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Using a measuring cylinder for the fixed volume or adding indicator in large amounts. The pipette supplies precision; too much indicator can obscure the colour change.

📎 Key Points to Remember
Pipette measures the flask volume; burette measures the delivered volume; indicator identifies the end-point.

notes.heading: Anion Tests
notes.body:
📌 Carbonate: add dilute acid; CO₂ turns limewater milky.
📌 Halides: acidify with dilute nitric acid, then add aqueous silver nitrate. Chloride gives white AgCl, bromide cream AgBr and iodide yellow AgI precipitates.
📌 Sulfate: acidify with dilute nitric acid, then add aqueous barium nitrate; a white BaSO₄ precipitate forms.
📌 Sulfite: acidified aqueous potassium manganate(VII) changes from purple to colourless.
📌 Nitrate: add aluminium foil and aqueous sodium hydroxide, then warm; ammonia turns damp red litmus paper blue.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Using hydrochloric acid to acidify a halide or sulfate test. It introduces chloride ions and can create a false precipitate; use dilute nitric acid.

📎 Key Points to Remember
Learn reagent → observation → ion, including the initial acidification step.

notes.heading: Cations with Sodium Hydroxide
notes.body:
📌 Add aqueous NaOH slowly, then to excess.
• Al³⁺: white precipitate, dissolves in excess → colourless solution.
• Ca²⁺: white precipitate, insoluble in excess.
• Cr³⁺: green precipitate, dissolves in excess → green solution.
• Cu²⁺: blue precipitate, insoluble in excess.
• Fe²⁺: green precipitate, insoluble in excess.
• Fe³⁺: red-brown precipitate, insoluble in excess.
• Zn²⁺: white precipitate, dissolves in excess → colourless solution.
• NH₄⁺: no precipitate; on warming, ammonia turns damp red litmus blue.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Reporting only the first precipitate. The excess-NaOH result distinguishes Al³⁺/Zn²⁺ from Ca²⁺ and Cr³⁺ from Fe²⁺.

📎 Key Points to Remember
Record precipitate colour AND solubility in excess; both are evidence.

notes.heading: Cations with Aqueous Ammonia and Flame Tests
notes.body:
📌 Aqueous ammonia gives useful contrasts: Cu²⁺ forms a blue precipitate that dissolves in excess to a deep-blue solution; Zn²⁺ forms a white precipitate soluble in excess. Al³⁺, Fe²⁺, Fe³⁺ and Cr³⁺ precipitates do not dissolve in excess ammonia; Ca²⁺ gives no precipitate with the dilute ammonia test.

🔑 Flame colours
Li⁺ crimson; Na⁺ yellow; K⁺ lilac; Ca²⁺ orange-red; Ba²⁺ pale green; Cu²⁺ blue-green. Clean the wire and use concentrated hydrochloric acid to prepare the sample as required by the practical method.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Confusing sodium's intense yellow with potassium's lilac, or assuming a flame colour identifies every ion in a mixture. One strong colour can mask another.

📎 Key Points to Remember
Use precipitation and flame tests as complementary evidence.

notes.heading: Gas Tests and Building a Conclusion
notes.body:
📌 Required gas tests
• NH₃: damp red litmus turns blue.
• CO₂: limewater turns milky.
• Cl₂: damp litmus turns red and is then bleached white.
• H₂: lighted splint gives a squeaky pop.
• O₂: glowing splint relights.
• SO₂: acidified aqueous potassium manganate(VII) turns from purple to colourless.

🔑 Logical identification
A positive result supports an identity only when the correct reagent and full observation are used. Combine tests where one result could fit several ions—for example, white hydroxide precipitates require an excess-reagent test.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Using a glowing splint for hydrogen or a lighted splint for oxygen. Hydrogen burns with a pop; oxygen supports combustion and relights a glowing splint.

📎 Key Points to Remember
State both the test and the positive observation, not just the gas name.

flashcards.definition: Draw in pencil and keep the initial solvent level below the sample spots.
flashcards.example: Pencil graphite does not dissolve and travel with the chromatography solvent.

flashcards.definition: A substance used after chromatography to make separated colourless substances visible.
flashcards.example: Spray after the solvent run when the separated substances have no colour.

flashcards.definition: Distance travelled by substance divided by distance travelled by solvent, measured from the baseline.
Volumetric pipette measures a fixed volume into the flask; burette delivers a measured variable volume; indicator shows the end-point.
flashcards.example: Add acid dropwise from the burette near the indicator colour change.

flashcards.definition: Acidify with dilute nitric acid and add silver nitrate: chloride white, bromide cream, iodide yellow precipitate.
flashcards.example: A cream precipitate identifies bromide ions.

flashcards.definition: Acidify with dilute nitric acid and add aqueous barium nitrate; sulfate gives a white precipitate.
flashcards.example: The white solid is barium sulfate.

flashcards.definition: Warm with aluminium foil and aqueous sodium hydroxide; ammonia produced turns damp red litmus blue.
flashcards.example: The litmus result detects ammonia, not nitrate directly.

flashcards.definition: Both form white precipitates soluble in excess aqueous sodium hydroxide.
flashcards.example: A white precipitate disappearing in excess gives a colourless solution.

flashcards.definition: A blue precipitate forms and dissolves in excess ammonia to give a deep-blue solution.
flashcards.example: The deep-blue solution distinguishes Cu²⁺ from metals with insoluble hydroxides.

flashcards.definition: Li crimson, Na yellow, K lilac, Ca orange-red, Ba pale green and Cu(II) blue-green.
flashcards.example: A lilac flame indicates potassium ions.

flashcards.definition: Oxygen relights a glowing splint; hydrogen gives a squeaky pop with a lighted splint.
flashcards.example: Do not swap the splint conditions.

flashcards.definition: Acidified aqueous potassium manganate(VII) changes from purple to colourless.
flashcards.example: Decolourisation is the positive observation in both tests.

questions.stem: Why is the baseline of a paper chromatogram drawn in pencil rather than ink?
choices: Pencil makes the solvent move faster
Ink reacts with every locating agent
Ink can dissolve and separate with the samples
questions.explanation: Ink contains soluble dyes that may travel up the paper and interfere with the chromatogram. Pencil graphite remains at the baseline.

questions.stem: Which apparatus should measure an accurate 25.0 cm³ portion of alkali into a conical flask?
questions.explanation: A volumetric pipette is designed to deliver one accurate fixed volume. The burette measures the variable volume delivered during titration.

questions.stem: A silver nitrate test gives a cream precipitate after nitric acid acidification. Which ion is present?
questions.explanation: Silver bromide is a cream precipitate. Silver chloride is white and silver iodide is yellow.

questions.stem: Which gas relights a glowing splint?
questions.explanation: Oxygen supports combustion and relights a glowing splint. Hydrogen gives a squeaky pop with a lighted splint.

questions.stem: A spot travels 3.6 cm while the solvent front travels 9.0 cm. What is its Rf value?
questions.explanation: Rf = substance distance ÷ solvent distance = 3.6 ÷ 9.0 = 0.40. Rf has no units.

questions.stem: What is the result when aqueous sodium hydroxide is added to Fe³⁺(aq)?
questions.explanation: Iron(III) ions form a red-brown iron(III) hydroxide precipitate that does not dissolve in excess sodium hydroxide.

choices: White precipitate with acidified barium nitrate
Cream precipitate with acidified silver nitrate
questions.explanation: After dilute nitric acid acidification, barium ions form insoluble white barium sulfate with sulfate ions.

questions.stem: A flame test gives a lilac flame. Which cation is indicated?
questions.explanation: Potassium gives a lilac flame. Sodium is yellow, calcium orange-red and copper(II) blue-green.

questions.stem: A solution gives a white precipitate with NaOH that dissolves in excess. Which pair of cations cannot yet be distinguished?
questions.explanation: Both Al³⁺ and Zn²⁺ give white hydroxide precipitates soluble in excess NaOH. Further evidence is required to distinguish them.

questions.stem: Why should dilute nitric acid, not hydrochloric acid, be used before a chloride test with silver nitrate?
choices: Nitric acid is always a stronger oxidising agent
Hydrochloric acid introduces Cl⁻ and could produce a false positive
Nitric acid removes all metal ions
questions.explanation: Hydrochloric acid itself supplies chloride ions, which can form white AgCl even if the original sample contained no chloride.

questions.stem: A colourless mixture has been separated by paper chromatography but no spots are visible. What should be used next?
choices: Universal indicator as a gas test
questions.explanation: A locating agent makes separated colourless substances visible after chromatography. It does not change the Rf measurement principle.

questions.stem: A cation gives a blue precipitate with aqueous ammonia, which dissolves in excess to a deep-blue solution. Identify it.
questions.explanation: Cu²⁺ gives blue copper(II) hydroxide initially and a deep-blue solution in excess aqueous ammonia.

questions.stem: A nitrate test is performed with aluminium foil and aqueous sodium hydroxide. Which positive observation confirms nitrate?
choices: Damp red litmus turns blue after warming
questions.explanation: Nitrate is reduced to ammonia on warming. Ammonia is alkaline and turns damp red litmus paper blue.

questions.stem: Two spots from an unknown match the heights of known substances A and B. What is the best conclusion under these conditions?
choices: The unknown is pure A only
The unknown contains substances consistent with A and B and is impure
The unknown contains every substance in the experiment
questions.explanation: Two spots indicate a mixture. Matching travel distances support identities A and B under the same conditions, but do not prove every possible component.

questions.stem: Near a titration end-point, how should the solution from the burette be added?
choices: Drop by drop while swirling until a permanent colour change
questions.explanation: Dropwise addition with swirling avoids overshooting the end-point. Start and final burette readings are both needed for the titre.
